```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4,
                      dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg", dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
has_sf <- requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)
has_cc <- requireNamespace("CoordinateCleaner", quietly = TRUE)
```

A gazetteer is a table of reference locations: the points or polygons a test compares each record with. The tests use three kinds:

- Points marking capitals, centroids, institutions, the GBIF headquarters and artificial hotspots.

- Polygons outlining land, urban areas, countries and species ranges.

- A table of genus habitats, used together with land polygons by the two habitat tests.

The package includes all of these except species ranges, which you supply.

To change the reference data for all tests at once, set `reference = "CoordinateCleaner"`. The tests then read the corresponding tables from your [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/) installation.

To change it for a single test, pass your own layer in the `gazetteers` argument of [`flag_occurrences()`](https://gillescolling.com/OccurrenceCleaner/reference/flag_occurrences.html). This argument does the job of the `ref` arguments in CoordinateCleaner's test functions.

This article shows how to filter, extend or replace the layer of a test and how a custom layer is recorded with the flags. Installation is covered in [Get started](OccurrenceCleaner.html). The polygon examples also need [sf](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/).

## A filtered point layer

A point layer is any data frame with longitude and latitude columns (`lon`/`lat`, `longitude`/`latitude` or `decimalLongitude`/`decimalLatitude`, in any case). The simplest custom layer is a subset of a shipped one. `reference_points()` returns the points of a proximity test with their attributes; for the institutions, `type` gives the kind of institution and `source` the registry each point comes from:

```{r points}
library(OccurrenceCleaner)

inst <- reference_points("institution")
head(inst[, c("name", "type", "source", "lon", "lat")], 3)
head(sort(table(inst$type), decreasing = TRUE))
```

The institution test uses the points whose `status` is not `"unconfirmed"`; [Reference data](reference-data.html#institutions) explains the status. A plant study, for example, may want to flag records at herbaria only, since a specimen georeferenced to a zoological museum is unlikely in a plant table, and use a wider buffer for them:

```{r herbaria}
used <- inst[inst$status != "unconfirmed", ]
herbaria <- used[used$type %in% "Herbarium", ]
nrow(herbaria)
near <- rbind(herbaria[1:3, ], used[used$type %in% "Museum", ][1:3, ])
x <- data.frame(species = "Quercus robur", decimalLongitude = near$lon + 0.005,
                decimalLatitude = near$lat)
f_all <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = "institution", buffers = list(institution = 1000))
f_herb <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = "institution", buffers = list(institution = 1000),
                           gazetteers = list(institution = herbaria))
data.frame(near = near$name, type = near$type, all = f_all$flag_institution,
           herbaria_only = f_herb$flag_institution)
```

Each record lies about 0.005 degrees (a few hundred metres) east of an institution: three herbaria, then three museums. The full table flags all six at a 1 km buffer. The herbarium table flags `r sum(f_herb$flag_institution)`, the records next to the herbaria.

The same works with the `extension` column. It is `TRUE` for points from sources CoordinateCleaner does not use; the rows with `extension` `FALSE` restrict a test to CoordinateCleaner's sources, as [Reference data](reference-data.html#extension-points) shows for the capitals. That article also lists the sources of every layer ([Institutions](reference-data.html#institutions) for the `source` and `master_source` columns of the institution table).

## An extended point layer

The two capital tables differ: the shipped table has the Factbook capitals unrounded and adds Natural Earth's alternative and official capitals, while [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/)'s has one point per country, rounded to 0.01 degrees. Their union flags records near either:

```{r union, eval = has_cc}
caps <- reference_points("capital")
both <- rbind(caps[, c("lon", "lat")], reference_points("capital", reference = "CoordinateCleaner"))
nrow(both)
y <- data.frame(city = c("Cape Town", "Naypyidaw", "Vienna"), decimalLongitude = c(18.42, 96.13, 16.37),
                decimalLatitude = c(-33.92, 19.75, 48.21))
data.frame(city = y$city,
           CoordinateCleaner = flag_occurrences(y, tests = "capital", reference = "CoordinateCleaner")$flag_capital,
           union = flag_occurrences(y, tests = "capital", gazetteers = list(capital = both))$flag_capital)
```

Other point sets fit the same way: regional capitals for a study in which collections were georeferenced to provincial seats, the field stations of a survey, or the coordinates a particular data provider uses as a default.

The institution table is one of them. The test uses CoordinateCleaner's institutions, some moved to the place Google Maps gives for the institution, and the points of other sources that a check has confirmed. The table also contains points that no check has confirmed, which the test leaves out:

```{r inst-status}
table(inst$status)
```

`gazetteers = list(institution = inst)` flags records near any point of the table, the unconfirmed ones included.

The Artificial Hotspot Occurrence Inventory (Park et al. 2023) behind the `aohi` test marks each point as a real observation site (`determination = TRUE`, for example a birding reserve) or an artificial aggregate of records (`FALSE`, for example a georeferencing default). A study that keeps records from popular sites can flag only the aggregates:

```{r aohi}
ah <- reference_points("aohi")
table(ah$taxon, ah$determination)
artificial <- ah[!ah$determination, ]
v <- data.frame(decimalLongitude = ah$lon[1:4] + 0.02, decimalLatitude = ah$lat[1:4])
data.frame(point = ah$notes[1:4], site = ah$determination[1:4],
           all = flag_occurrences(v, tests = "aohi")$flag_aohi,
           aggregates = flag_occurrences(v, tests = "aohi", gazetteers = list(aohi = artificial))$flag_aohi)
```

The four records lie about 2 km from the first four bird hotspots, all of them birding sites, so the full inventory flags them and the aggregates-only table does not.

## Polygon layers

Polygon layers are `sf` or `sfc` objects of POLYGON or MULTIPOLYGON geometries in longitude and latitude (EPSG:4326). For `sea`, the polygons are the land: a record outside every polygon is flagged. That makes `sea` with a custom layer a test for "outside the study area":

```{r study-area, eval = has_sf}
area <- sf::st_sfc(sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(c(9.5, 46.4), c(17.2, 46.4), c(17.2, 49.0),
                                             c(9.5, 49.0), c(9.5, 46.4)))), crs = 4326)
z <- data.frame(decimalLongitude = c(16.37, 11.40, 8.54, 19.04), decimalLatitude = c(48.21, 47.26, 47.37, 47.50))
flag_occurrences(z, tests = "sea", gazetteers = list(sea = area))$flag_sea
```

The first two points (Vienna and Innsbruck) lie inside the box; the last two (Zurich and Budapest) lie outside. For `urban`, polygons likewise define the areas to flag, such as a city's built-up area mapped in finer detail than Natural Earth provides.

For `country_mismatch`, polygons also carry country or territory codes in columns named `iso_a2`, `iso_a3`, `adm0_a3` or `code` (case-insensitive). Each record's code is checked against all available code columns. The following example uses two territories with their own codes:

```{r countries, eval = has_sf}
terr <- sf::st_sf(
  code = c("XA", "XB"),
  geometry = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(c(0, 0), c(10, 0), c(10, 10), c(0, 10), c(0, 0)))),
                        sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(c(10, 0), c(20, 0), c(20, 10), c(10, 10), c(10, 0)))),
                        crs = 4326))
w <- data.frame(decimalLongitude = c(5, 15, 15, 25), decimalLatitude = 5, countryCode = c("XA", "XB", "XA", "XA"))
flag_occurrences(w, tests = "country_mismatch", gazetteers = list(country_mismatch = terr))$flag_country_mismatch
```

The third record is in territory XB with code XA, the fourth outside both territories, so both are flagged.

## Species ranges

The `range` test flags records outside the range polygons of their species, such as IUCN range maps. The layer is an `sf` object with one or more polygons per species and a species column, named like the record's species column or `species`, `binomial` or `sci_name`. Each species gets an index of its own polygons, so overlapping ranges of different species do not interfere; species without a polygon are not tested:

```{r range, eval = has_sf}
ranges <- sf::st_sf(
  species = c("Bufo bufo", "Bufo bufo", "Lacerta viridis"),
  geometry = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(c(-10, 36), c(30, 36), c(30, 60), c(-10, 60), c(-10, 36)))),
                        sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(c(30, 40), c(60, 40), c(60, 60), c(30, 60), c(30, 40)))),
                        sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(c(5, 40), c(30, 40), c(30, 52), c(5, 52), c(5, 40)))),
                        crs = 4326))
r <- data.frame(species = c("Bufo bufo", "Bufo bufo", "Bufo bufo", "Lacerta viridis", "Lacerta viridis",
                            "Lacerta viridis", "Rana arvalis"),
                decimalLongitude = c(10, 45, -20, 15, 15, 15, 100),
                decimalLatitude = c(50, 50, 50, 45, 52.5, 55, 10))
data.frame(r, outside = flag_occurrences(r, tests = "range", gazetteers = list(range = ranges))$flag_range,
           outside_100km = flag_occurrences(r, tests = "range", gazetteers = list(range = ranges),
                                            buffers = list(range = 100000))$flag_range)
```

The toad at 45 E lies in the second of its two polygons and is kept; the one at 20 W lies in the Atlantic, outside both. The lizard at 52.5 N lies half a degree, about 55 km, north of its range: it is flagged without a buffer and kept with the 100 km buffer. The lizard at 55 N is 3 degrees north and stays flagged under both. *Rana arvalis* has no polygon and is not tested.

## A genus habitat table

The habitat tests `sea_nonmarine` and `land_marine` use `reference_habitat()` to look up each record's genus in the Interim Register of Marine and Nonmarine Genera. You can supply your own table with columns `genus`, `marine` (`TRUE` for exclusively marine genera, `FALSE` for nonmarine genera) and optionally `kingdom`. For example, you can classify a genus whose habitat the register leaves unspecified:

```{r habitat}
h <- reference_habitat()
h[h$genus %in% c("Larus", "Zostera"), ]
mine <- rbind(h, data.frame(kingdom = "Plantae", genus = "Zostera", marine = TRUE))
x <- data.frame(kingdom = "Plantae", genus = "Zostera", decimalLongitude = 16.37, decimalLatitude = 48.21)
flag_occurrences(x, tests = "land_marine")$flag_land_marine
flag_occurrences(x, tests = "land_marine", gazetteers = list(habitat = mine))$flag_land_marine
```

The register marks seagrass (*Zostera*) as marine but leaves its freshwater and terrestrial flags empty, so the shipped table does not class it and its records are not tested; classed as only marine, a record of it in Vienna is flagged.

## Recording the layer

A custom layer is indexed once per call, and its size and an MD5 checksum of its coordinates are written into the reference label of the output:

```{r label}
f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = "institution", gazetteers = list(institution = herbaria))
attr(f, "occ_reference")
```

The checksum identifies the exact table, so two analyses that report the same label used the same points. For streamed input the label is stored in the output directory, and a rerun into that directory with a different custom layer stops with an error instead of mixing flags from two layers.

## Comparison with CoordinateCleaner

```{r cc-map, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  CoordinateCleaner = c("cc_cap(ref = ...)", "cc_cen(ref = ...)", "cc_inst(ref = ...)",
                        "cc_sea(ref = ...)", "cc_urb(ref = ...)", "cc_coun(ref = ..., ref_col = ...)",
                        "cc_iucn(range = ...)", "cc_aohi(taxa = ...)", "(none)"),
  OccurrenceCleaner = c("gazetteers = list(capital = points)", "gazetteers = list(centroid = points)",
                        "gazetteers = list(institution = points)", "gazetteers = list(sea = polygons)",
                        "gazetteers = list(urban = polygons)", "gazetteers = list(country_mismatch = polygons)",
                        "gazetteers = list(range = polygons)",
                        "gazetteers = list(aohi = subset of reference_points(\"aohi\"))",
                        "gazetteers = list(habitat = genera)"),
  check.names = FALSE))
```

OccurrenceCleaner recognises common longitude and latitude column names and matches records against every country-code column present. [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/) requires specific coordinate names, such as `capital.lon`, `centroid.lon` or `decimalLongitude`, and its [`cc_coun()`](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/reference/cc_coun.html) uses one code column selected with `ref_col`.

With the same reference points and polygons, both packages produce the same flags except near buffer boundaries, as described in [Compatibility with CoordinateCleaner](coordinatecleaner.html). Package tests check this agreement for `institution`, `sea` and `range`.
